§1.4a — Phases of the Moon: The Moon Clock

Unit 1: Intro to the Cosmos · Astronomy

Watch the Moon for a month and it changes shape every night: a thin sliver, a half, a full circle, then back again, every 29.5 days. And it is not only a night thing. On your way to school on Monday morning, look south: a thin crescent Moon will be up in broad daylight.

Why does it change shape? And why is it up at 8 am some weeks and at midnight in others? People have told stories about that for as long as there have been people. Today we build a scientific model instead.

Today: the phase of the Moon tells you the time.

Moon drawn from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter map (NASA SVS)

1 · Myths: explaining the unexplainable

What did people do in the evening before there were screens? They looked up, and they made myths to explain the unexplainable. The Moon got more stories than anything else in the sky.

Greek myth: Apollo and Selene

Apollo, the Greek Sun god, propels the Sun's chariot across the sky, bringing daylight, while Selene, the Moon goddess, bathes the night in moonlight. Apollo is linked with many human tales and is known for his music and prophecy, while Selene's role is more otherworldly, overseeing the Moon's passage through the night sky.

In groups: come up with your own myth. A good one has to explain three things you have seen: why the Moon changes shape, why the pattern repeats, and why the Moon is sometimes up in the daytime. Keep your list. A scientific model has to explain the same three things, and it has to make predictions.

Eight phases

The Moon has eight phases, and they always come in the same order over the 29.5-day lunar month. While the lit part grows the Moon is waxing; while it shrinks the Moon is waning. Less than half lit is a crescent, more than half is gibbous. The two half-lit phases are the quarters: the Moon is a quarter of the way around its orbit, even though you see half of the face lit.

The eight phases, as you see them from Portland
Top row: waxing, New to Full. Bottom row: waning, Full back to New. In the northern hemisphere a waxing Moon is lit on the right.

    Build a scientific model

    A myth only has to be a good story. A scientific model has to explain the data and predict what happens next. Here is the Moon data any model must explain:

    Moon data for building a scientific model
    1. Repeatable: the same 8 phases, in the same order.
    2. 29.5 days for one full cycle, the synodic period.
    3. A correlation between phase and time: each phase rises and sets at its own time of day.

    Fact 3 is the one people miss. In class we read the times off Stellarium. New and Full are filled in. Predict the two quarters before you check: the pattern is already in the first two rows.

    Phase vs rising and setting time
    PhaseRising timeSetting time
    Notice that every phase is up for about 12 hours, and each step from one quarter to the next phase shifts the times by 6 hours. Your myth has to explain that. So does our model.

    Why? Four facts

    Four facts explain all of the Moon data.

    1. The Sun is far. Light from a lamp across the room spreads out (it diverges). The Sun is so far away, about 400 times farther than the Moon, that by the time its light reaches us the rays are parallel. That means the Earth and the Moon are lit from the same direction.

    Move the light away: diverging becomes parallel

    2. The Moon goes around the Earth, counterclockwise when you look down on the North Pole. Earth spins counterclockwise too. That is why the Sun, the Moon and the stars all rise in the east and set in the west.

    3. The far side from the Sun is dark. The 50% of the Moon and of the Earth that faces the Sun is lit. The other 50% is night.

    4. You can see 180° of sky at any moment, from the eastern horizon over your head to the western horizon. Your horizon is the line that cuts the sky you can see from the sky blocked by the Earth under your feet.

    Shaded Earth with your horizon: drag yourself around
    Measure: how fast does the clock turn?
    Earth turns 360° in 24 hours. How many degrees in one hour?° per hour
    The eight phases sit 45° apart around the orbit. How many hours does Earth take to turn 45°?hours

    The Moon Clock

    Put the four facts together and look down on the North Pole with the Sun off to the left. Earth is the face of a clock and you are its hand. When you face the Sun it is noon. A quarter turn later (counterclockwise) the Sun is setting behind you: 6 pm. Facing away from the Sun is midnight, and the next quarter turn is 6 am.

    The Moon Clock. Wherever the Moon sits on its orbit, read the clock time at that spot: that is when the Moon is highest in your sky. It rises 6 hours earlier and sets 6 hours later. Each phase step is 45° around the clock, which is 3 hours.
    Frank goes out at midnight and looks straight up: the Full Moon is highest. It rose at 6 pm and sets at 6 am.
    Nancy goes out at noon and looks straight up: the New Moon is highest, lost in the Sun's glare. It rose at 6 am and sets at 6 pm.
    Drag the Moon around its orbit and drag the person around Earth. Try Your eyes to stand in Portland and look south. Challenge gives you moon-clock problems.
    Measure: read the clock

    Count the steps from New, then use 3 hours per step from noon.

    1. Look straight at the lamp. What time is it?
    2. Turn until the lamp is just out of sight over your left shoulder. Are you awake? What time is it?
    3. Move the Moon to make it New. Then Full. Then Third Quarter.
    4. Hold a First Quarter Moon. At what time of day can you first see it?

    Moon clock problems

    Every problem is the same three steps: find the Moon on the clock, find yourself on the clock, and count 3 hours per step. Try each one before you reveal it.

    Ex. 1 to 5 · Moon clock

    Ex. 1. The Moon is Full and setting. What time is it?

    Reveal
    A Full Moon is highest at midnight (Frank). It sets 6 hours later: midnight $+ 6$ hr $= \boxed{6\ \text{am}}$.

    Ex. 2. Here is the view from above the North Pole. What phase do you see, what time is it, and where is the Moon in your sky?

    Reveal
    The Moon is a quarter turn counterclockwise from New, so it is a $\boxed{\text{First Quarter}}$. You are standing at the 6 am spot on the clock: $\boxed{6\ \text{am}}$. A First Quarter is highest at 6 pm, so it rises at noon and sets at midnight. At 6 am it is below the horizon: you cannot see it.

    Ex. 3. It is noon, and the Moon is a Waning Crescent. Where is it in the sky?

    Reveal
    A Waning Crescent is 7 steps from New: $12\ \text{pm} + 7 \times 3\ \text{hr} = 9\ \text{am}$ the next morning. So it is highest at 9 am, and noon is 3 hours later: halfway down in the western sky.

    Ex. 4. From Earth the Moon is a Third Quarter. What phase of the Earth does an astronaut on the Moon see?

    Reveal
    Look back from the Moon at the Earth. The astronaut sees half of Earth's lit side too, but on the other side: $\boxed{\text{a First Quarter Earth}}$. Earth's phase is always the opposite one, because when you see little of the Moon's day side, the Moon sees a lot of Earth's.

    Ex. 5. A Full Moon rose three hours ago. What time is it?

    Reveal
    A Full Moon rises at 6 pm (6 hours before it is highest at midnight). $6\ \text{pm} + 3\ \text{hr} = \boxed{9\ \text{pm}}$.
